articles.title: The Solar Pump Hangover: What Broke India’s Former Renewable Stock Darlings?
articles.description: There is a curious contradiction at the heart of India's solar-pump industry today. The market for solar irrigation has never looked more established. PM-KUSUM has created a huge installed base, with 9.30 lakh standalone pumps sanctioned and 8.40 lakh installed under Component B as of August 31, 2026. The government is also working on the next phase of the programme, with a proposed new component around agrivoltaics. Yet three of the most prominent listed names associated with the boom — Shakti Pumps, GK Energy and Oswal Pumps — have seen their market valuations suffer spectacularly As of September 24, 2026, Shakti Pumps was at ₹472.15, down about 46% from its 52-week high of ₹877.70. GK Energy was at ₹125.10, almost 48% below its ₹239.45 peak. Oswal Pumps was at ₹280.25, roughly 65% below its ₹789.95 52-week high. The numbers are striking, but the real story is not the stock-price decline. It is the question that has emerged underneath it: Was the market valuing these companies as enduring clean-energy franchises when a significant part of their extraordinary growth was actually the product of a government-driven procurement cycle? The answer will determine what happens next. The first crack: growth is no longer translating into the same margins Shakti Pumps offers the clearest illustration. The company reported FY25 revenue of ₹2,516 crore, up 83.6% year-on-year, while PAT jumped 188.2% to ₹408.4 crore. It was the kind of earnings acceleration that naturally attracts a premium valuation. But FY26 turned out very different. Consolidated revenue rose further to ₹2,722 crore, while PAT fell to ₹257.6 crore from ₹408.4 crore. EBITDA declined from ₹620 crore to ₹446.5 crore. And the latest quarter reinforces the concern. In Q1 FY27, revenue climbed 37.9% year-on-year to ₹858.7 crore. Operating profit, however, fell 42.3% to ₹82.9 crore, while net profit was ₹51.6 crore. This is an important distinction. The problem is not necessarily lack of demand. The problem is what that demand is worth. The extraordinary margin expansion of FY24-FY25 had encouraged investors to think of higher profitability as structural. The subsequent numbers suggest at least part of it was cyclical. That changed the valuation equation. A company growing revenue 30%-40% while margins contract sharply is a very different proposition from a company growing revenue at 30%-40% while retaining 20%-plus operating margins. The tender trap This is where the structure of the solar-pump industry becomes important. PM-KUSUM was designed to accelerate deployment through central financial assistance, state participation and beneficiary contributions. Component B targets 14 lakh standalone solar agriculture pumps. That created an enormous market. But government procurement also tends to create intense competition. The customer has significant purchasing power. Vendors compete for large orders. And once multiple manufacturers and EPC companies have built capacity, winning volume can become more important than preserving price. Oswal Pumps' latest numbers illustrate the problem. Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue fell 7.9% year-on-year to ₹473.6 crore, but EBITDA fell about 42%, to ₹82.5 crore. The operating margin declined to around 17.4%, from 28.4% a year earlier. Analysis of the quarter attributed much of the pressure to competitive bidding and roughly 9% lower realisations. That is the fundamental vulnerability of the model: A large order book does not automatically mean a high-quality order book. Volume visibility can coexist with pricing pressure. And when component costs, employee expenses or project costs rise, the margin squeeze can be disproportionately large. GK Energy shows another side of the problem GK Energy's numbers are actually much stronger on the surface. Q1 FY27 revenue rose 55.5% year-on-year to ₹505.2 crore, operating profit increased 44%, and net profit climbed nearly 60% to ₹59.7 crore. So why has the stock fallen so sharply? The answer lies partly in the composition of that revenue. In FY25, around 83.83% of GK Energy's revenue came from EPC of solar-powered agricultural water-pump systems sold directly to beneficiaries under PM-KUSUM. The company's IPO-related disclosures explicitly identified the risk that failure to extend PM-KUSUM beyond March 31, 2026, or replace it with comparable state schemes, could materially affect its business and financial performance. That is not an indictment of GK's execution. It is a statement about concentration risk . Investors can simultaneously believe that GK is growing rapidly and believe that the earnings deserve a lower valuation multiple because so much of that growth remains linked to a particular policy ecosystem. This is one of the most important lessons from the sector's correction: Business momentum and valuation momentum are not the same thing. The PM-KUSUM cliff that isn't necessarily a cliff The industry's challenge is made more complicated by the transition from PM-KUSUM's original framework. The MNRE scheme was formally designed to run until March 31, 2026, with Component B targeting 14 lakh standalone pumps. But the government's current position does not suggest that solarisation of agriculture is being abandoned. The national dashboard shows that deployment has continued to scale, while the government has indicated that the next phase of PM-KUSUM is being considered. For manufacturers, however, a transition between schemes can be almost as important as the eventual policy outcome . Tender schedules can move. State allocations can be delayed. Orders can bunch up. And most importantly perhaps, payments are invariably delayed. And companies that have invested in manufacturing capacity cannot simply switch factories on and off according to quarterly tender activity. That creates a difficult operating environment even when the long-term demand thesis remains intact. The three companies are now trying to escape the pump-only box This explains perhaps the most interesting strategic development across the sector. All three companies are diversifying. But they are doing so in different ways. Shakti: become a broader manufacturing platform Shakti Pumps has perhaps the most ambitious diversification plan. Its strategy goes beyond pumps into motors, inverters, structures and other components, while it is also pursuing solar-cell and module manufacturing. Its FY25 disclosures outlined a proposed 2.2 GW solar cell and module manufacturing project. The attraction is obvious. Instead of being dependent on one product category and one government-led market, Shakti could theoretically participate across several parts of the solar value chain. But diversification is not automatically value creation. Solar manufacturing is capital-intensive and intensely competitive. Capacity is being added rapidly across India, while module and cell economics remain sensitive to global supply, technology and pricing. Shakti is therefore trading one kind of concentration risk for another: Less dependence on pumps, but potentially greater capital intensity. Oswal: follow the solar customer beyond irrigation Oswal's strategy is more focused on EPC diversification. The company is expanding into rooftop, utility and commercial-and-industrial solar, alongside its established pump business. The strategy is already producing tangible orders. In September, Oswal won a ₹273.19 crore Telangana rooftop-solar project covering 46.7 MW across government schools. That matters because rooftop EPC provides an avenue to build revenue outside agricultural pump procurement. But again, the key question isn't whether the company can win orders. It is whether these orders can generate attractive margins and cash flows at scale. GK: storage could change the proposition GK Energy's diversification into battery energy storage is arguably the most strategically interesting. The company has secured a 150 MW/300 MWh BESS project in Maharashtra, with the project expected to provide approximately ₹42.84 crore of annual revenue over a 15-year period once operational. That introduces something the solar-pump EPC model lacks to the same degree: long-duration contracted revenue visibility. It does not remove execution, financing or counterparty risk. But it potentially changes the nature of the business. GK is no longer simply asking investors to value another batch of pump installations. It is beginning to offer exposure to an entirely different part of the energy-transition infrastructure market. But will investors reward diversification? That is the billion-rupee question. Historically, Indian markets have not rewarded diversification simply because management announces it. Investors eventually look through the presentation to the financial statements. For these three companies, five indicators will matter. 1. Revenue diversification What percentage of revenue comes from businesses outside PM-KUSUM-linked pumps? 2. Margin quality Are new businesses producing sustainable margins, or are they simply replacing one low-margin growth business with another? 3. Cash conversion Does EBITDA translate into operating cash flow? 4. Return on capital Are new factories and capacities producing sufficient returns? 5. Customer diversification Can the companies win meaningful business from C&I, utilities and private customers, rather than remaining overwhelmingly dependent on government programmes? These questions are likely to matter more to investors than the absolute size of the next pump order. The numbers tell a useful story Three listed solar-pump plays: where the business stands Metric Shakti Pumps GK Energy Oswal Pumps FY25 revenue ₹2,516 cr ₹1094 cr ₹1432 cr FY25 PAT ₹408 cr ₹133 cr ₹289 cr FY26 revenue ₹2,722 cr ₹1715 cr ₹2,064 cr* FY26 PAT ₹258 cr ₹204 cr ₹376 cr Q1 FY27 revenue ₹859 cr ₹505 cr ₹474 cr Q1 FY27 YoY revenue +37.9% +55.5% -7.9% Q1 FY27 PAT ₹51.6 cr ₹59.7 cr ~₹54 cr Q1 FY27 margin trend Sharp contraction Relatively resilient Sharp contraction Key exposure Pumps + solar manufacturing PM-KUSUM EPC Pumps + EPC Major diversification Cells/modules, solar ecosystem Rooftop + BESS Rooftop/C&I/utility solar *FY26 figures and the latest quarterly figures should be treated as reported consolidated figures where available; Oswal's financial filings are the definitive source for final publication reconciliation. The table captures the central paradox. GK is still growing extremely rapidly. Shakti is still growing revenue rapidly. Oswal is still winning sizeable solar orders. Yet all three are being valued more cautiously. That tells us that the market's concern is not simply about demand. It is about earnings quality and durability. The correction is not uniform. Oswal has suffered the largest drawdown from its recent high, while Shakti and GK have both lost almost half their peak value. The market is therefore not merely repricing the sector as a whole; it is differentiating between business models and earnings trajectories. Shakti's latest operating margin is dramatically below the levels achieved during its earlier earnings boom. Oswal has also seen a major year-on-year compression, while GK has so far shown greater resilience. That does not establish that GK will permanently have better economics. It does show why investors are beginning to distinguish between the companies. Shakti is moving towards a broader solar manufacturing ecosystem. GK is adding rooftop solar and storage. Oswal is building out rooftop, utility and C&I EPC. The companies are all effectively saying the same thing to investors: Do not value us solely on solar pumps. The market's response, however, is equally clear: Then prove it in the numbers. What happens next? The most interesting possibility is that the current correction ultimately proves healthy for the sector. The first phase of India's solar-pump industry was about creating scale. The next phase has to be about creating quality. That means moving from: government scheme → tender → order → installation → revenue towards: technology + manufacturing + diversified customers + recurring revenue + cash generation. The companies that make that transition successfully could eventually command a very different valuation framework. But there is a warning embedded in that opportunity. Diversification can destroy value if it becomes an excuse for indiscriminate capital expenditure. A pump manufacturer entering cells, modules, rooftop EPC, storage and other businesses is not automatically a better company. It is simply a company with more businesses.The market will decide whether that is diversification or dilution based on returns. The solar-pump opportunity isn't dead. The easy money may be. India's agricultural solarisation story remains compelling. PM-KUSUM has already demonstrated demand at scale, and the government's interest in extending the programme suggests the policy objective remains relevant. But the stock-market version of that story has changed. Investors once focused heavily on the size of the opportunity and the speed of order inflows. They are now looking at pricing, margins, working capital, cash conversion and capital allocation. That is arguably a more mature way to value the sector. The companies themselves now have an opportunity to demonstrate that they are more than PM-KUSUM beneficiaries. If they can diversify without sacrificing returns, convert profits into cash and build meaningful non-pump businesses, the current correction could eventually be remembered as a valuation reset during a period of strategic transformation. If they cannot, the market may continue to treat them as cyclical beneficiaries of government procurement. But one thing is clear: India's solar-pump market has not necessarily broken. The old investment thesis has. And the next chapter will be decided not by how many pumps India installs, but by how much sustainable, cash-generating value the companies installing them can create.

articles.title: BMC rolls out minimum standards for Mumbai civic hospitals
articles.description: Uniforms, biometric attendance, housekeeping checks, tendering, and peer reviews among measures under new Minimum Essential Standards

articles.title: From Fibre to Future: Weaving Sustainability into India's Textile Growth
articles.description: Giriraj SinghAs India targets a US$350 billion textile and apparel industry by 2030, sustainability is moving from the margins to the centre of its competitiveness strategy. For a sector spanning fibre, yarn, fabric, processing, apparel, technical textiles and made-ups, sustainability is increasingly becoming a question of competitiveness, market access and responsible growth.When Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that “The World is adopting the vision of Fashion for Environment and Empowerment, and India can lead the way in this regard,” he pointed to a transformation increasingly visible across India’s textile landscape.The textile sector is a major employment engine, directly supporting over 49 million livelihoods. Its domestic market is valued at about US$196 billion and is projected to reach US$250 billion by 2030, while India is targeting US$100 billion in textile exports by the same year.The Ministry of Textiles’ sustainability agenda reflects this dual reality. It is built around a simple proposition: India should not have to choose between growth and sustainability. Instead, cleaner production, resource efficiency, circularity and responsible manufacturing are set to become the foundation of the textile sector’s next growth chapter.Why sustainability has become a competitiveness issueGlobal brands are setting increasingly ambitious sustainability targets for their supply chains. Consumers are showing greater interest in reused, repaired and recycled products, while policymakers in major export markets are introducing requirements around environmental performance, recycled content, traceability, chemicals, water and energy use. India’s climate commitments—including 500GW of non-fossil energy capacity, 50% of energy requirements from renewables and net zero emissions by 2070—are also steering the textile sector towards a low-carbon growth trajectory. For Indian exporters, sustainability is therefore moving beyond a peripheral compliance issue and becoming an integral part of industrial competitiveness.India also starts from a position of strength, with a large manufacturing base, diverse raw materials, technical capabilities, an established recycling and reuse ecosystem, a growing start-up landscape and a wide network of clusters, research institutions and industry associations. Circularity is not entirely new to India. Traditions such as rafugari, kantha, godhadis, chindi durries and khesh weaving have embedded repair, reuse and repurposing in communities for generations.India’s hosting of the World Circular Economy Forum 2026 further reflects this larger shift, bringing governments, industry, innovators and experts together to turn ideas into partnerships and scalable solutions.Turning textile waste into a circular opportunityOne of the clearest areas to put circularity into practice is textile waste. A Ministry study from 2026, covering 15 states and more than 250 stakeholder interactions, estimated annual textile waste generation at 70.73 lakh tonnes. More than 70 per cent is already recovered and routed into recycling, downcycling or upcycling streams, with recovery of pre-consumer waste exceeding 95 per cent.The larger gap is post-consumer waste, where collection, segregation and economically viable recovery systems remain less developed. The study estimated that India’s textile recycling market could reach about US$3.5 billion by 2030, with opportunities across collection, sorting, fibre recovery, recycling, upcycling, repair and sustainable manufacturing, with the potential to generate around one lakh green jobs.The Ministry is moving beyond quantifying the problem to building the infrastructure and market mechanisms needed to close the loop. Textile Recovery Facilities are being piloted in multiple cities, while textile-waste mapping is identifying the need for stronger collection and sorting systems and policy solutions for blended and non-recyclable materials. A textile-waste management pilot in Navi Mumbai, implemented by the Textiles Committee in partnership with Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation, Saahas Foundation and women’s self-help groups, diverted more than 3,323 kg of textile waste monthly from landfill and incineration, reached over 12,000 families and installed more than 80 collection bins. It also produced over 1,000 sample and upcycled products. Through a partnership between the Textiles Committee, Government e-Marketplace (GeM) and SCOPE, certified upcycled textile products are being brought into public procurement. Thirty-one upcyclers have been certified under the Upcycled Textile Mark, with 27 categories and 40 products live on GeM, helping create an assured market for circular products.Cleaner production: water, energy and chemicalsCircularity is only one part of the sustainability story. Much of the environmental footprint of textiles is created during manufacturing and processing, making water, energy and chemicals equally important. The agenda of eliminating hazardous chemicals is being taken up through a major programme with UNIDO, the Global Environment Facility and other partners. The project aims to reduce hazardous chemicals while improving energy, water and greenhouse-gas performance. Its targets include reducing 10,530 tonnes of toxic chemicals directly and 21,000 tonnes indirectly, while mitigating 147,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent directly and 294,000 tonnes indirectly. It is also designed to directly reach 40,000 people, 60 per cent of whom are expected to be women. At the infrastructure level, sustainability is being built into the sector’s future industrial geography. Seven PM MITRA Parks, with an expected investment of about US$10 billion, are envisaged with integrated water, wastewater and common processing infrastructure.From pilots to scale: policy, technology and MSMEsFor sustainability to become mainstream, pilots must move into factories and clusters. This is particularly important because a large part of the textile ecosystem comprises MSMEs, which may face constraints in accessing technology, finance, data and technical expertise. The Ministry constituted an ESG Task Force in July 2023, bringing together government bodies, industry associations, chambers, multilateral agencies, innovators, brands and academia. Its work focuses on harmonised certification, cluster handholding, awareness and capacity building, sustainable fashion technology, and the use of artificial intelligence and digitalisation for data and traceability. The ESG Task Force has supported the EU-India Resource Efficiency & Circular Economy Initiative (EU-I RECEI), implemented through GIZ, covering a national assessment of textile waste, a circular economy roadmap for Tamil Nadu, an MSME toolkit for Panipat and a standard operating procedure for Textile Recovery Facilities. A separate UNEP-led programme is providing life-cycle assessment and eco-innovation training and technical assistance to SMEs in the Surat and Karur clusters.Technology and innovation are also long-term enablers. The National Technical Textiles Mission supports research into waste-to-fibre technologies and conversion of textile waste and bio-residues into advanced green materials. At IIT Delhi’s Panipat campus, the Atal Centre of Textile Recycling and Sustainability is undertaking research and technology transfer, including recycling heat-resistant aramid fibre waste used in defence and aerospace applications. At Bharat Tex 2026, sustainability-focused research on traceable hemp fibre, circular business models and wheat straw as a forest-free alternative for man-made cellulosic fibres further highlighted the breadth of innovation emerging around the sector.Tex-Eco: sustainability within the growth architectureThe Union Budget 2026–27 provided a strong policy signal. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced an Integrated Programme for the labour-intensive textile sector, with Tex-Eco placing sustainability alongside fibre security, manufacturing expansion, traditional clusters, handlooms, handicrafts and skilling—not as a separate environmental programme, but as part of the sector’s growth architecture. The proposed Tex-Eco Initiative brings together four strategic pillars: resource recovery and recycling infrastructure; water stewardship and decarbonisation; institutionalising sustainability and building capability; and innovation, digital enablement and knowledge systems. Textile Recycling Mega-Hubs and Textile Recovery Facilities would support collection, sorting, grading and routing of textile waste. Water and decarbonisation measures would support ZLD, renewable energy, low-emission boilers and resource-efficient technologies. An India Sustainability Mark is proposed to strengthen market credibility, alongside assurance, compliance, capacity building and demand generation.Building an ESG ecosystemBehind these interventions is a broader institutional shift. A dedicated Sustainability Section within the Ministry of Textiles acts as a focal point for sustainable and circular practices, resource efficiency, environmental impact reduction, green technologies and responsible production. The government is positioned not only as regulator, but also as facilitator, leader and implementing partner. The ESG agenda also goes beyond the environmental dimension. Worker welfare, formalisation, green jobs and a just transition sit alongside decarbonisation, water stewardship, chemical safety and circularity, while governance priorities include standards, traceability, disclosure, certification and assurance.The next chapterIndia’s textile sustainability journey is entering a critical phase, with the focus now on stronger post-consumer collection, recycling infrastructure, resource-efficient manufacturing, commercialisation of green technologies, credible measurement and traceability, and stronger markets for recycled and upcycled products. A proposed Sustainability Alliance would bring together government, UN agencies, financial institutions, industry, MSMEs and academia around these priorities.The direction is increasingly clear: sustainability must work for a factory owner as much as for the environment, for an exporter as much as the consumer, and for a large integrated park as much as for a small enterprise. This can improve resource productivity, unlock access to demanding global markets, spur new businesses around recycling and green technologies, and generate employment.For a nation on track to nearly double its textile and apparel market by 2030, sustainability is not about slowing growth. It is about powering the next wave of growth—cleaner, more circular, more resilient and ultimately more competitive.The author is the Union Minister of Textiles. The views expressed are personal.
